The use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in various applications has been well established. However, there's still a lack of understanding about how GNNs learn and where they go wrong. This research aims to investigate the transfer learning in GNN architectures, focusing on the role of architecture design in adapting to new datasets. We've developed ArchTrans, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates how different GNN architectures perform on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks. Our study reveals that GNN architectures can indeed learn from each other, but this learning is highly dependent on the specific task and the source of the data. We've also identified key architectural elements that contribute to transfer learning, such as the type of aggregator used, the existence of multiple GNN layers, and the use of attention mechanisms. Our findings provide valuable insights for designing GNN architectures that can effectively learn from diverse sources of data. We've made our benchmark and code available for public use.

We investigate the spin susceptibility of Heisenberg magnets on a simple cubic lattice in the paramagnetic phase and find that it follows a specific power law in relation to momentum. This power law is determined by a universal exponent that depends on the dimension of the spin but not on the specific structure of the lattice. We calculate this exponent by examining the momentum and frequency dependence of the dynamic spin structure factor in three-dimensional classical and quantum Heisenberg models using Monte Carlo simulations. We discover that the exponent is influenced by a non-analytic term in the structure factor and that it can be used to determine the critical exponents of the order parameter scaling in the ferromagnetic and nematic stages of these models. We also explore the generalisation of our findings to other types of magnets and discuss their implications for the scaling of the spin wave energy in these systems. Artificial neural networks, used in image recognition tasks, often rely on visual features from the center of an image, making them susceptible to adversarial attacks that exploit this reliance by manipulating the center pixels. To counter this vulnerability, we suggest a novel neural architecture inspired by the biological visual system's on-off center-surround response. This system responds strongly to visual stimuli both at the center and at surrounding areas, and weakly to stimuli absent from both areas. The proposed network, called OCS-NET, is designed to focus on both central and peripheral image features, and thus is more resistant to adversarial attacks targeting the central region. OCS-NET's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets, both in normal conditions and under attack. The results show that OCS-NET significantly outperforms the baseline model in terms of accuracy under attack, and also achieves better results in adversarial robustness and generalization. Furthermore, OCS-NET's improved performance is accompanied by lower computational requirements. To our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize the on-off center-surround visual response to enhance the resilience of machine learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that PESTO outperforms existing methods in NER tasks for code-mixed text, and its effectiveness is further validated through an ablation study. Our research highlights the importance of considering the inter-lingual relationships within a sentence when processing code-mixed text, and we provide a comprehensive resource for code-mixed NLP research. To overcome this limitation, we present a new framework for visual relocalization that leverages 3D surfel mapping technology to enhance feature detection and description. By utilizing 3D models, our approach generates pseudo-images representing 3D scenes, allowing for more effective feature extraction and matching. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art techniques using the KITTI dataset and achieve significant performance improvements, with a 10% increase in localization accuracy in sequence 11 and 20% in sequence 21, and comparable results for sequence 19 and 20. Additionally, our approach demonstrates better robustness to different feature extractors and geometrically consistent noise. This paper presents a framework choice method for Chain Event Networks using Maximum A Posteriori estimation within a Bayesian framework. Network choices are evaluated based on their fit to observed data, and a metric called Bayesian Information Criterion is employed to make selections. In contrast to traditional Bayesian approaches that rely on model averaging, this method focuses on the most likely network choice. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in a Bayesian setting by applying it to the 2011 Mississippi River Floods and the 2014 Alberta Floods, showing that it produces results comparable to full Bayesian inference. Moreover, we propose a method to estimate event likelihoods based on expert-provided severity data. This method is validated through a case study of the 2016 Fort McMurray Wildfires in Canada. Furthermore, we investigate how to integrate additional data types, such as social media and geospatial information, to enhance network fit. Ultimately, this method is expected to facilitate the selection of Chain Event Networks for a variety of emergency events. A software package, called BECMAN, is developed to implement this method and facilitate its use. It is available for download at https://github.com/USC-GEAR/becman.

However, current methods struggle with understanding the intended SQL query when
given ambiguous input, often relying on external guidance like database schemas.

Our method involves two key components: first, we develop a pre-training task to
improve SQL query generation without relying on labels; second, we use a novel
training technique to fine-tune the model for the cross-domain task.
Our approach demonstrates superior performance on the xT2SQL dataset, outperforming
existing methods by a significant margin in terms of both exact and fuzzy match
metrics. Notably, our model achieves a high exact match rate of 24.8% on the

This benchmark, named the 'Recurrent Learning' (RL) challenge, centers around a basic task: predicting the next event in a sequence of continuous values. This approach, called 'Temporal Learning' (TL), involves using the time-based information from the input sequence to inform the prediction of the next event. This approach not only improves the models' performance but also enhances their ability to learn over time. The RL challenge offers a valuable opportunity to assess the ability of deep learning models to learn over time and to develop more effective methods for temporal understanding. Stochastic Gradient Ascent (SGA) is a widely used method for exploring the posterior distribution in Bayesian inference and optimization, but its effectiveness can be significantly impacted by noisy gradient estimates. Current SGA techniques often rely on assumptions of well-calibrated noise and fail to account for noise variability. In this study, we investigate the use of the Expected Information Gain (EIG) as a robust metric for evaluating noisy gradient quality. By leveraging EIG, we develop a dynamic adjustment strategy that accelerates SGA exploration in favorable conditions and prioritizes exploration over exploitation in high-noise scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in adapting to changing noise levels and outperforming accelerated gradient methods in noisy environments. Additionally, we provide theoretical justifications for our approach and show that it achieves a linear exploration-exploitation trade-off under optimal conditions. Furthermore, we extend our method to the scenario where the noise level is unknown and develop an adaptive version that adjusts its exploration-exploitation strategy based on posterior uncertainty estimates. In real-world applications, our approach successfully identifies better models for hyperparameter tuning and achieves state-of-the-art results in Bayesian model averaging. A well-developed robotic skill set is essential for executing various tasks, and object manipulation is a critical component of this. Grasping, a fundamental aspect of object manipulation, is complex due to the need for precise prediction of grasp success and force application. Current robotic grasping methods face limitations, primarily due to the restricted availability of training data. To address this issue, we introduce DexGraspNet, a comprehensive simulated dataset featuring 1,000,000 grasp poses and object models. Our approach employs a novel dataset synthesis technique, leveraging procedural generation to create diverse object variations and grasp poses. Additionally, we develop a data filtering method to ensure high-quality grasp poses. Our evaluation demonstrates that DexGraspNet outperforms existing datasets in terms of grasp success rates. Furthermore, we employ DexGraspNet to train a grasp policy, which achieves a 0.83 AUC score on the Cornell dataset, surpassing the state-of-the-art performance. Our dataset is available for download at https://github.com/autonomousvision/DexGraspNet.

A novel, free-breathing motion-adjusted four-dimensional (4D) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) MRI sequence has been developed for use in the abdominal region. This sequence utilizes a combination of a low-flip-angle radiofrequency pulse and a modified acquisition timing to minimize respiratory effects, without the need for a respiratory sensor. This new sequence has the potential to improve the assessment of abdominal organs through MRI. We investigate the potential of pre-training a semantic segmentation model using a task unrelated to segmentation, such as monocular depth estimation, to improve performance. Our hypothesis is that depth and semantic information are interdependent, and thus, a model trained on depth can capture essential features beneficial for segmentation. We demonstrate that pre-training on a depth model and then fine-tuning on a segmentation task can yield better results than traditional approaches, including pre-training on a segmentation task. Notably, this benefit is more pronounced in scenarios with limited training data. Our study also reveals that the advantage of depth pre-training diminishes as the amount of training data increases. We attribute this outcome to the fact that depth and segmentation are correlated, and thus, a model can leverage this relationship to extract valuable features even with limited supervision. Our findings suggest that depth pre-training can be a valuable alternative or supplement to conventional segmentation pre-training techniques. The code for our experiments is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/krishnateja95/depth-pretraining. Moreover, we have created a comprehensive dataset consisting of synthetic images with ground truth depth and semantic labels, which can be accessed via https://github.com/krishnateja95/depth-segmentation-dataset. This dataset can serve as a valuable resource for developing and evaluating models that integrate depth and semantic information. Ultimately, our research aims to inspire the development of novel unsupervised pre-training methods that can enhance the performance of semantic segmentation models. In the display advertising realm, where revenue is generated through auctions, companies face budget constraints and must strategically choose the time and quantity of bids to maximize revenue. This problem is known as online bidding with a budget, and existing solutions typically involve two stages: first predicting and adjusting ad values, and then using those estimates to make bidding decisions. This method, which uses a non-parametric statistical technique, has been shown to outperform traditional methods in both revenue and accuracy terms. Furthermore, our approach can be easily integrated into existing bidding systems and is highly scalable. In the realm of reinforcement and imitation learning, reward learning stands out for its potential to adapt rewards to various agents without the need for environment modifications. However, reward functions created through learning often fail to align with human goals, necessitating human input to correct these errors. This process is labor-intensive and requires a time-consuming analysis of the agent's actions, which can be costly. Our approach involves utilizing visually-assisted ranking to group trajectories into similar paths, allowing us to pinpoint agents' mistakes and correct their errors more effectively. By focusing on trajectory clusters rather than individual actions, we reduce the time and effort required for human input, making our method more efficient and scalable. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on a simulated robotic task and a real-world video game environment, showcasing its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing human input costs. Our results also highlight the importance of considering trajectory clusters rather than individual actions when designing reward learning algorithms. This presentation delves into various searches for supersymmetry (SUSY) particles using a vast dataset collected by the CMS experiment in 13-TeV proton-proton collisions. With a dataset of 138 fb$^{-1}$ of data, the presentation covers a range of SUSY searches, including those for strong and electroweak production of supersymmetric particles. It particularly focuses on the CMS searches for gluinos, squarks, sleptons, charginos, neutralinos, and winos, including in final states with multiple, missing transverse particles accompanied by various jets and leptons. These searches are further examined using simplified models and are interpreted within theoretical models such as R-parity violating scenarios and the Coannihilation planes of the pMSSM. Neural rendering has become a versatile tool for complex rendering tasks, but it typically requires access to extensive scene and material information, which isn't always available. To address this limitation, we propose Brightness Field Neural Rendering, a method that uses a simplified neural network to simulate the appearance of objects in low-light conditions, requiring only a single input image and ambient lighting. Our approach builds on the concept of brightness maps by introducing a neural model that learns to combine them with ambient lighting to produce high-quality images, even in the absence of direct lighting. We also extend this concept to apply to other rendering tasks, such as material editing and image translation, without requiring any additional training data. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in these applications, while using significantly fewer model parameters. For example, our material editing model requires just 0.3 MB to produce high-quality results, a 100-fold reduction compared to other methods. Despite the abundance of research, there is still a lack of in-depth understanding of transferability, with existing knowledge mainly consisting of anecdotal evidence. This study aims to provide a more comprehensive insight into transferability by examining two widely-held assumptions. The first assumption is that domain similarity directly affects transferability, while the second assumes that model similarity is the primary factor. Our findings indicate that these assumptions do not entirely hold true and that other factors, such as dataset and network design, play a more crucial role in determining transferability. This study also introduces a new metric to quantify the impact of dataset on transferability, revealing that the source and target datasets significantly influence the outcome. Furthermore, our analysis of network design reveals that using a common dataset for training different models can result in similar transferability outcomes, regardless of the models' differences. This study's findings provide valuable insights for practitioners to improve the transferability of their models. In e-commerce, a specific task known as Item Retrieval (IR) is crucial for enhancing user shopping experiences by recommending items. However, existing methods that apply computer vision and natural language processing to solve IR often fall short due to limitations in their training data and model design. To address these limitations, we introduce ECoPre, a novel pretraining framework for IR that leverages multiple sources of data, including product descriptions, image captions, and insight data. By developing a dual encoder architecture that can process both visual and linguistic information, ECoPre is able to effectively capture the complex relationships between product features and user queries. Furthermore, we introduce a novel training objective that enables the model to learn more effective item representations and improve retrieval accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of ECoPre over existing baselines on multiple IR benchmarks. Notably, our model achieves a significant relative improvement of 10.3% in offline metrics and 8.5% in online metrics, and outperforms a strong baseline in online A/B testing. Moreover, we showcase the effectiveness of ECoPre in real-world scenarios through the deployment of our model on a major e-commerce platform. The source code of ECoPre is publicly available at https://github.com/bytedb/economic-pre.

The PALEOCCENE experiment aims to detect low-energy nuclear recoils using $^{19}$Al$^+$ ions within a deep ultra-high vacuum Penning trap at the Laboratori Nazionale del Gran Sasso. By leveraging the ions' 565 keV alpha-decay signature from $^{19}$Ne captured within the ion, the experiment will utilize a novel technique to identify nuclear recoils resulting from interactions with dark matter. Given the ions' extremely low count rates, the PALENEOCENE will employ an innovative method combining individual event analysis with machine learning algorithms to differentiate between signal and background events. With a projected background rate of 0.1 events per day in the 1 keV recoil energy range following three years of data collection, the PALEOCCENE will be capable of setting world-leading limits on dark matter cross-sections in the 1-10 GeV/c$^2$ mass range. The PALEOCCENE will also be the first experiment to directly measure the ionization quenching factor for color centers within a solid. In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, agents learn to take actions that maximize cumulative rewards relative to a specified goal. However, achieving this goal can be hindered by ambiguities arising from open-ended goal descriptions. To address this challenge, we investigate how language-based communication affects goal understanding and develop a new training method for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning that accounts for ambiguous goal representations. Our approach involves training a joint model that simultaneously generates actions and clarifies goal-related concepts, leveraging both intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards. Experimental results demonstrate that our method efficiently learns to adapt to changing, verbally stated goals in complex navigation scenarios. Moreover, we find that the agent's ability to identify relevant goal features is transferable across different environments and communication partners. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of more robust and adaptable reinforcement learning agents capable of handling uncertain or ambiguous information. The application of quantum computing in machine learning has led to the development of quantum neural networks, which utilize quantum mechanics to enhance learning processes. This study aims to explore how quantum states are processed within quantum neural networks, examining both the noise inherent in quantum systems and the effects of measurement on the networks' behavior. We've found that the noise in quantum states can hinder the networks' ability to converge, while the effects of measurement can either improve or impede the networks' performance, contingent upon the initial state and the specific problem being solved. This research provides a foundation for understanding the behavior of quantum neural networks and may lead to the development of new algorithms capable of leveraging quantum states to solve complex problems. We've also proposed a potential method for generating quantum-inspired solutions to classical problems, which could potentially yield more accurate results than traditional classical approaches. This paper presents a novel application of factor models to address the challenge of mortality forecasting. Our approach yields a model that surpasses the ONS model and the original time-invariant factor model in performance, while also providing a clear and interpretable explanation for the observed improvements in forecasting accuracy during the COVID-19 pandemic. Notably, our results demonstrate that time-varying factor loadings are particularly essential for modeling periods of significant change, such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2008 financial crisis. Furthermore, we identify distinct factors driving mortality that are unique to these events, highlighting the importance of considering multiple perspectives when analyzing data. Our findings also reveal that the time-varying factor loadings are primarily responsible for the observed improvements in forecasting accuracy, underscoring the significance of adapting to changing conditions in modeling mortality. This research contributes to the development of a robust and adaptable framework for forecasting UK mortality, which can be easily extended to other countries and regions. Moreover, our approach offers a versatile method for modeling time-varying phenomena in a wide range of fields. The effectiveness of concept-based search queries heavily relies on the accurate incorporation of relevant concepts. In response to a user's query, suggested concepts can enhance the relevance of search results, but their improper inclusion may detract from relevance. To address this, a novel approach called Concept-Assisted Question Answering (CAQA) has been developed, which involves incorporating concepts into existing search queries to boost relevance. However, the optimal way to modify a query remains uncertain, with human experts often inserting concepts into the query without a clear strategy. To resolve this, a proposed method, Strict Concept Placement (STRICT), automatically determines the most effective position for concepts within the query based on the query's semantic meaning. By framing this task as a retrieval-based search phrase identification problem, STRICT leverages pre-existing search phrases to determine the optimal placement of concepts. Experimental results demonstrate that STRICT outperforms existing methods, with a 10% improvement in average performance on a benchmark dataset. Moreover, a thorough analysis of the approach reveals that STRICT's performance is particularly robust in scenarios with limited training data. By analyzing the structural patterns within STEM domains, we can identify and extract relevant mathematical entities, which can then be used to create a comprehensive knowledge graph representation. This representation serves as a powerful tool for capturing complex relationships between documents and their underlying mathematical concepts. By incorporating edge information, which reflects the diverse ways in which entities interact, we can develop a more comprehensive understanding of the STEM domain. In online marketplaces, the issue of offer extension arises when a buyer seeks to
propose a contract to a seller, yet hesitates due to uncertainty about the
seller's willingness to accept it. To resolve this uncertainty, the buyer may
request additional information or propose an alternative offer to present to
another seller. This problem is referred to as the "reliable matching" issue, and
it can be viewed as a decision-making task where the buyer chooses an action
involving information request or offer presentation. We analyze this decision task
as a stochastic shortest path problem with uncertain rewards and examine how
different decision-making methods, including myopic and far-sighted approaches,
influence the overall expected time to find a matching. Furthermore, we investigate
the relationship between the structure of the reward function and the properties of
the optimal policy, and we also provide a method for approximating the optimal
stochastic matching policy in a finite state and action space setting. Lastly, we
demonstrate the applicability of our findings to real-world scenarios through two
case studies. One case study involves the sale of used goods through online market
platforms, and the other case study focuses on the issue of offer extension in
organ-donor matching. In both cases, the optimal policy is non-myopic and takes
into account the presentation of alternative offers to enhance matching chances. 
This research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the reliable
matching issue and its practical applications in various domains. Moreover, it
highlights the significance of considering multiple offers in matching scenarios. 
The research also reveals that relying solely on a single offer may not always
guarantee the best matching outcome. In certain situations, presenting additional
offers can significantly improve the likelihood of a successful match. We hope that
this research will inspire further investigation into the reliable matching issue and
its broader implications for decision-making processes involving offer extension. 
Ultimately, the research aims to contribute to a better understanding of the
reliable matching problem and its applications in real-world contexts.

To overcome these drawbacks, we propose SummScore, a comprehensive evaluation metric that uses a Cross-Encoder to assess summaries holistically. This model-based approach enables automatic creation of high-quality reference annotations without relying on human-annotated datasets. Furthermore, SummScore outperforms existing metrics in evaluating summarization quality across various domains and can adapt to different domains without requiring new annotations. Our experiments demonstrate SummScore's superiority in evaluating summarization quality, and it is available for download at https://github.com/nyu-dl/SummScore.

We introduce BEVFusion, a straightforward and adaptable 3D-2D fusion framework that combines camera and LiDAR data within a single output coordinate system. By utilizing a LiDAR-centric coordinate system, we simplify the integration process of these two data sources. Our approach, BEVFusion, is based on the BEV transformer, which fuses LiDAR and camera data in this coordinate system. This allows for the generation of a unified output coordinate system, which can be used for various downstream applications. Our approach is versatile, allowing it to be used with a range of back-end modules, such as LiDAR-only, camera-only, and combined perception modules. Furthermore, we have developed a novel method for self-supervised pre-training, which enables the BEVFusion module to function effectively without labeled data. Our approach has been successfully applied to several tasks, including LiDAR-only, camera-only, and combined perception modules, achieving state-of-the-art results on the Waymo Open Dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/autoturing/BEVFusion.

Design conversations are a crucial aspect of collaborative design processes, 
enabling designers to share their ideas and expertise with clients. However, 
recording and analyzing these conversations can be a complex task due to their 
unpredictable nature and the varied perspectives of those involved. To address 
this challenge, we have developed a new approach that utilizes natural language 
technologies to automatically identify design conversations during meetings, 
without the need for prior categorization or specific meeting agendas. Our 
approach has been successfully applied to a real-world dataset from a leading 
design firm, allowing us to accurately conclude design conversation mining 
without the need for manual intervention. Our results demonstrate the 
effectiveness of our method in accurately identifying design conversations and 
concluding the mining process, and we believe that our approach has the 
potential to greatly improve the efficiency of design conversation mining.

Furthermore, we visualize the overlapping cluster structures using interactive visualizations to facilitate interpretation. Overall, our approach provides a new way to model complex data structures and it's a valuable tool for data analysts to uncover hidden patterns in their data. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that FIRe-GAN outperforms existing fusion methods across multiple metrics, including the Ssim, Ms-ssim, Lp, and Fmeasure, thereby showcasing its potential as a valuable tool for a range of wildfire-related visual analytics applications. Furthermore, we showcase the practical applications of FIRe-GAN in real-world scenarios through two case studies. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to an unprecedented global health crisis, prompting widespread research into categorizing patients to contain the spread of the disease. To aid in the rapid diagnosis and containment of the virus, a novel two-phase approach utilizing BERT attributes is proposed for COVID-19 categorization. Subsequently, a fine-tuned BERT model is used to generate clinical reports and extract essential features, which are then combined with image and report probabilities to produce the final diagnosis. To evaluate the efficacy of this method, a dataset comprising 5,000 patients was employed, yielding a remarkable accuracy of 0.96 and F1-score of 0.96 for positive cases. Furthermore, the approach achieved a high F1-score of 0.83 for negative cases. The exceptional results of this method are attributed to the use of a BERT-based model, which enables the efficient extraction of relevant information from clinical reports and image probabilities. The proposed approach is envisioned to be a valuable tool for healthcare professionals in the rapid diagnosis and containment of the disease. Historical texts, found in documents from the 16th century onwards, pose a unique challenge to modern NLP systems due to their linguistic and formatting differences from contemporary text. The task of part-of-speech (POS) annotation is particularly susceptible to errors introduced by earlier labeling efforts. To address these issues in historical collections, we propose a novel approach to POS labeling that leverages the advantages of machine learning algorithms. By framing the task as a set-valued forecasting problem, we can incorporate the inherent ambiguity of historical language and account for annotation inaccuracies. The resulting model, based on a conditional random field, enables the simultaneous prediction of multiple POS tags for each sentence, effectively mitigating the impact of annotation errors. The proposed approach is evaluated using two historical collections from the 17th and 19th centuries, and the results demonstrate its ability to produce reliable outputs even in the presence of flawed annotations. Furthermore, we investigate the effectiveness of combining the proposed method with existing correction techniques to improve the overall quality of the outputs. Furthermore, the study demonstrated that TD-COVIDNet can effectively detect COVID-19 from noisy images, and even at low capsule sizes, it can achieve high accuracy. The study also employed a capsule network to identify the most significant features contributing to COVID-19 detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that "Rapid Sinkhorn II" can be combined with "Rapid Sinkhorn I" to achieve an even higher level of accuracy while maintaining a computational complexity of O(n logN). The effectiveness of this approach is validated through a comparison with state-of-the-art methods in solving optimal transport problems. Through collective learning, robots adjust their behavior to achieve shared objectives, such as exploring and mapping complex environments, while maintaining their unique identities and autonomy. By leveraging these principles, robots can effectively collaborate and make decisions as a cohesive team, even in situations where they encounter unexpected challenges and obstacles. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we present several case studies involving simulated robots that work together to explore and map complex environments. These case studies highlight the importance of individual and collective autonomy in achieving shared objectives, while also showcasing the unique characteristics and behaviors of each robotic entity. For individuals with visual impairments, navigating unfamiliar spaces can be particularly challenging due to limited visual perception and reliance on auditory and tactile senses to build a mental map. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach, the Hierarchical Topological Map (HiTMap), which uses spatial and structural data from buildings to create a navigable diagram. By analyzing floor plans and incorporating key features along with their connections, HiTMap constructs a simplified and intuitive network of nodes and edges. This diagram representation is designed to facilitate navigation by providing a high-level overview of a space, allowing users to choose their path and stay on course. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted a usability study with visually impaired participants, who demonstrated improved navigation skills with HiTMap compared to conventional maps. This research offers practical solutions for creating visual aids that can be easily accessed through tactile or auditory means. A recent study on Named Entity Recovery (NER) through NLP pretraining has demonstrated the capability of models to automatically learn and identify named entities without human supervision, relying solely on NLP pretraining objectives. However, this approach has a significant drawback: it fails to provide any insight into the specific terms contributing to identifying actual entities. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method called Term Importance Feedback (TIF), which aims to enhance NLP pretraining models for NER by incorporating a feedback mechanism that assigns importance weights to individual terms based on their ability to contribute to identifying actual entities. By incorporating these importance weights into NLP pretraining objectives, TIF enables the model to learn more effectively and improve its overall performance. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that TIF outperforms existing state-of-the-art NER methods, achieving a substantial improvement of up to 4.4 points in F1 score. Additionally, our analysis reveals that TIF achieves better generalization and more robust performance in low-resource settings and when dealing with out-of-vocabulary entities. To facilitate future research, we release our code and dataset on GitHub for public access. An extended version of this paper is available on arXiv.

The extracted requirements also facilitated the development of test cases, resulting in a 0.43 similarity between the test cases and the extracted requirements, comparable to the developer's performance. The study's findings suggest that natural language processing can be an effective approach to derive software specifications from informal text sources. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to analyze the spin states of magnetic adatoms and clusters on superconductors by combining the Anderson and Shiba models with the Rusinov model. This unified approach accounts for the spin-dependent interactions between the localized magnetic impurities and the host material's conduction electrons within the context of the relativistic Bloch states and the quasi-particle excitations that occur above the critical temperature. This novel theory is exemplified through its application to Mn adatoms and dimers on the Nb(110) surface, where the calculated spin-state energy spectra are in close agreement with experimental findings. Furthermore, the theory's predictions regarding the spin-dependent interactions between the magnetic impurities are consistent with the observed phenomena, where the presence of one magnetic impurity suppresses the spin-dependent interactions between adjacent impurities. This theoretical framework provides a foundational understanding of the complex many-body interactions that occur between localized spins and superconducting hosts, thereby facilitating the exploration of novel spin-based quantum devices. We examine the Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) problem in the context of Reinforcement Learning (RL). IRL seeks to infer a reward function that an agent's learned policies aim to maximize. In this study, we investigate the IRL problem within the framework of linear bandits. We first establish that in linear bandits, IRL is feasible when a reward function exists in a compact set, but becomes computationally challenging (possibly requiring superpolynomial time) when the dimension of possible reward functions increases, even with a known upper bound. To address this challenge, we propose a new algorithm, called IRL-ADAM, which iteratively refines an initial reward estimate using a stochastic gradient descent approach. We demonstrate that IRL-ADAM converges to a local maximum of the true reward function with a convergence rate of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\log D} / T)$. Notably, IRL-ADAM is the first algorithm capable of handling IRL in linear bandits with an unknown upper bound on the dimension $D$ of possible reward functions, and its sample complexity is sublinear in $T$, the number of iterations. In virtual reality (VR) throwing interactions, the point of release is a critical parameter that can be challenging to determine. This study examines how inaccuracies in estimating the point of release affect throwing movements and identifies two primary issues: overrotation and arm velocity deviations. To address these concerns, we propose FauxThrow, a novel interaction technique that utilizes a virtual object's mass and velocity to suggest an optimal release point, minimizing the risk of impact and ball trajectory deviations. The results demonstrate that FauxThrow can significantly reduce ball trajectory deviations and improve user satisfaction. Furthermore, FauxThrow can be integrated with existing VR throwing systems without substantial modifications. The findings and implementation guidelines from this study can inform the development of future VR throwing applications. This research investigates the creation of highly efficient NMT models that can operate on low-end hardware, such as mobile devices, including those with limited resources like Android phones and tablets. To achieve this, we explore two techniques: knowledge distillation and quantization, which compact existing MT models into smaller, more lightweight models. Our study compares the performance of these two methods in terms of translation accuracy, using a range of existing NMT models and a standard translation task. The results show that knowledge distillation produces more translationally accurate models, but these models are not as compact as those produced by quantization. To address this, we propose a hybrid approach that combines the two techniques, resulting in a significant improvement in model efficiency without compromising translation accuracy. The study also highlights the challenges associated with training MT models on low-end hardware, including the fragility of the quantization process. To mitigate this fragility, we propose a new training method that uses a combination of gradient updates, which stabilizes the quantization process and improves the quality of the resulting MT models. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method, which results in MT models that are both accurate and efficient. The study also highlights the importance of carefully selecting the teacher model for knowledge distillation, as well as the impact of data augmentation on the quality of the resulting MT models. Overall, our study provides new insights into the creation of efficient MT models, which can operate on low-end hardware, and identifies areas for future research. The study also showcases a range of publicly available code and pre-trained models that can be used to create efficient MT models. This tutorial showcases MMLSpark, an open-source Python package for scalable machine learning and deep learning development. The package is built on top of Apache Spark's MLlib library and incorporates deep learning functionality, along with integration with Spark's DataFrames and the global caching capabilities of DataSets. The tutorial will cover the key features of MMLSpark, including its support for Keras model training and inference, as well as caching and batching with Spark's DataFrames and DataSets. The tutorial will also demonstrate the use of Spark's caching and batching capabilities for data preparation and pre-processing, and showcase MMLSpark's support for distributed training and testing. The tutorial will culminate in a demonstration of how to deploy a trained model in real-time using Spark's DataFrames and the MLlib decision tree classifier. The tutorial will be accompanied by a live demonstration of MMLSpark in action, showcasing its capabilities on Azure. This paper proposes a method to select between APs and Extenders based on channel usage by utilizing the feedback from the network's Master Controller, which is provided through the IEEE 802.11k/v standard. This information is then analyzed by a controller that makes informed decisions on device placement to minimize congestion and improve overall network performance.
